context: Construction of Object Shelter (sarcophagus) began within days of the accident; early phase involved helicopter drops of lead dolomite sand boron; concrete pumping to Unit 4 pool and reactor shaft; main structural work began May-June 1986
notes: Sarcophagus construction was the most radiologically hazardous construction project in history; workers measured in minutes per shift near reactor; remote-controlled cranes and dozers used where possible; human workers required for critical connections
source: OECD-NEA Chernobyl 1996; IAEA Safety Reports Series 2006; Sich 1994 Science

context: Object Shelter officially completed November 30 1986; ~7 months from accident to completion; construction involved ~250000 workers in 1986 phase of 600000 total cleanup workers
notes: The 7-month completion was remarkable given radiological conditions; Soviet engineers improvised solutions to unprecedented challenges; building over an active radioactive source; no precedent for this type of work
source: OECD-NEA 1996; INSAG-7; Soviet documents; IAEA TECDOC-1477

context: ~250000 of the ~600000 total Chernobyl liquidators directly involved in Shelter construction in 1986; workers rotated frequently (minutes-to-hours per shift near reactor) to limit doses; dose limit nominally 25 rem (250 mSv) per worker
notes: Soviet records indicate many workers exceeded the 250 mSv limit; retrospective dosimetry (EPR; FISH; RADRUE) shows significant fraction received 300-1000+ mGy; see retrospective_dosimetry_methods_REAL.csv for dose reconstruction challenges
source: UNSCEAR 2008 Annex D; retrospective_dosimetry_methods_REAL.csv; IAEA Safety Reports

context: ~400000 tonnes of concrete poured; ~7000 tonnes of steel structures; total structure weight ~1 million tonnes including reactor ruins and rubble within; footprint approximately 200m × 100m; height ~70m above ground
notes: Concrete was poured using modified construction equipment with extended booms; workers could not approach within 100m of reactor face for most operations; quality of concrete work was compromised by remote pouring and radiation effects on workers

context: Approximate external dimensions: 200m east-west (along Unit 3-4 axis); 100m north-south; maximum height ~70m; includes enclosure of reactor building, turbine hall segment, and reactor hall
notes: Exact dimensions vary by measurement reference; reactor hall (central section) is the most radiologically hazardous area; the western wall was the most problematic to seal due to proximity to Unit 3
source: IAEA TECDOC-1477; EBRD; Novarka NSC design documents

context: Object Shelter had >1000 m² of gaps and openings from its 1986 construction; result of remote pouring inability to properly seal joints; gaps allowed: radioactive dust escape; birds nesting inside (further mixing contamination); rain/snow ingress; approximately 900 m³/day of water infiltration through Shelter
notes: Water infiltration = major concern: water dissolves Sr-90 from fuel particles inside; radioactive water leaches to soil and groundwater below; water monitoring wells around shelter perimeter show elevated Sr-90; dust transport outside Shelter is secondary contamination pathway
source: IAEA TECDOC-1477; Bugai 2022 Sci Rep; EBRD Shelter Fund reports

context: Steel roof trusses over Unit 4 central hall deteriorating by 1992; corrosion in high-humidity high-radiation environment; Shelter roof is built partly atop rubble of original Unit 4 roof; structural assessments from 1990s showed collapse risk; 1993: reinforcement of some trusses
notes: Roof collapse scenario was the primary motivating driver for the New Safe Confinement; a roof collapse would release a large pulse of radioactive dust; estimated 2% annual probability of major collapse by 2003 without intervention
source: IAEA TECDOC-1477; EBRD Shelter Fund; various structural engineering assessments 1997-2006

context: Interior of Object Shelter contains: fuel particles (hot particles); graphite fragments; corium dust; radioactive concrete dust from reactor explosion; total inventory estimated tens of TBq of fine respirable dust; maintained slightly negative pressure in NSC to prevent outward migration
notes: Dust lofting inside Shelter is triggered by: temperature changes; vibration; any structural movement; NSC design provides containment in case of Shelter collapse and dust release

context: Approximately 900 m³/day of water (precipitation) enters Shelter through gaps and roof; water contacts fuel particles and corium; Sr-90 dissolved into water; radioactive water accumulates in basement rooms and leaches to groundwater
notes: NSC installation reduced precipitation ingress to near zero; however water already accumulated inside Shelter remains; active water management systems operate inside NSC; Bugai 2022 shows groundwater Sr-90 plume extending from Shelter to cooling pond
source: Bugai 2022 Sci Rep doi:10.1038/s41598-022-22842-5; IAEA TECDOC-1477; EBRD reports

context: SIP (Shelter Implementation Plan) launched 1997 by EBRD with 45 donor nations; NSC was largest single sub-project (~€1.5B of €2.1B total SIP budget; NSC design competition won 1997 by Bouygues + Vinci consortium; design finalized 2001-2003
notes: SIP also included: stabilization of Object Shelter structure; demolition of unstable sections; waste management infrastructure; dust suppression systems; monitoring equipment; NSC was the crown jewel of the program

context: Novarka JV (50% Vinci + 50% Bouygues Construction); French consortium selected for design-build contract awarded 2007; construction began in earnest 2010; two halves of arch built on east and west sides of sarcophagus then joined and slid over
notes: Choice of arch design (vs alternative box/dome designs): allows future dismantling of old sarcophagus by overhead cranes operating inside; provides 100+ year working life; negative pressure maintained inside to prevent dust release

context: NSC arch: height 108m (taller than Statue of Liberty); span 162m (widest moveable structure ever built); length 257m along east-west axis; steel arch weight ~36000 tonnes; total structure ~29000 tonnes additional steel and equipment; internal volume ~506000 m³
notes: The NSC is the largest moveable land structure ever built; records: largest steel arch; largest single moving structure; built in two halves because arch could not be assembled over sarcophagus (radiation too high)
source: EBRD; Novarka; WNA; Guinness World Records entry

context: NSC arch pushed (slid) over Object Shelter on November 29 2016; operation took 15 hours; rails with sliding shoes (teflon pads on stainless rails); pushed by hydraulic jacks; moved 327 meters to final position over sarcophagus; precision required: <5cm positional accuracy
notes: November 29 2016 sliding was the final major construction milestone; official inauguration July 2019 after fitting out internal equipment; NSC became operational for remote monitoring in 2019
source: EBRD; Novarka; multiple news sources November 2016

context: NSC equipped with: 3 overhead bridge cranes (150 tonne + 50 tonne + 3 tonne capacity); remote-controlled dismantling tools; dust suppression system; dehumidification system; radiation monitoring sensors; ventilation maintaining negative pressure; personnel access airlocks
notes: The cranes and remote tools enable future dismantling of old Object Shelter without human workers entering the highly contaminated zone; timeline for dismantling: 2028-2035 planned for most hazardous sections

context: NSC construction cost €1.5 billion; funded by 45 donor nations through EBRD Chernobyl Shelter Fund; major donors: European Union (~€400M); France Germany USA Japan; full SIP program €2.1 billion including Shelter stabilization and other works
notes: €1.5B for single structure; per-unit cost comparable to large conventional nuclear power plant; justified by: preventing collapse; enabling eventual full decommission; demonstrating international cooperation on nuclear safety

context: NSC designed for minimum 100 year service life; allows: Cs-137 to decay by ~10 half-lives (fraction of original); corium to cool further; dismantling technology to develop; permanent geological repository to be sited and built; by 2116 Cs-137 reduced to <0.1% of 2016 level
notes: 100-year design enables the dismantling of Unit 4 contents under controlled conditions; matches timeline for ISF-2 dry cask storage (also 100 years); decommission target 2064 refers to lower-contamination structures; Unit 4 core dismantling extends beyond 2064
source: EBRD; CHNPP decommission schedule; rbmk_fuel_specifications_REAL.csv; isotope_decay_timeseries_REAL.csv

context: February 14 2025: Russian drone strike hit NSC; caused ~6 meter diameter breach in outer membrane (not inner containment); structural arch itself not damaged; breach allows weather ingress but not immediate radiological release risk
notes: Breach identified during regular inspection; EBRD and donor nations immediately pledged repair fund; €31 million repair fund established; full restoration target 2030; inner NSC membrane intact; radiation monitoring inside NSC showed no elevated readings
source: cez_research_2022_2025_REAL.csv; NEA Chernobyl 2024 status report; multiple sources Feb 2025

context: Repair fund: €31M from EBRD donor nations; preliminary engineering assessment complete; access to repair location limited by ongoing conflict; restoration target 2030; NSC continues to function as containment during repair period
notes: Represents second major wartime damage after Oct 2025 16-hour power loss (resolved without radiological consequence); war impact on Chernobyl management ongoing; IAEA monitoring efforts constrained; see cez_research_2022_2025_REAL.csv

context: Elephant's Foot corium in basement Room 217/2 still emits ~34 µSv/h as of 2026 (down from 10000 R/hr = 100 mSv/h in 1986); see corium_fcm_physics_REAL.csv for detailed corium data; neutron flux in Room 305/2 stable since 2022
notes: NSC keeps weather out and maintains negative pressure; human workers can briefly access some areas of old Shelter for inspection; inner contaminated zones still inaccessible without heavy shielding; full dismantling awaits future remote technology
